summary: Gives guidance on using external pre-shared keys (PSKs) with TLS 1.3. It lists the security properties PSKs can provide under certain assumptions, shows how breaking those assumptions leads to attacks, and offers advice for applications. It also covers PSK use cases and how keys are provisioned. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An external pre-shared key is a secret that two devices already hold before they connect, used by TLS to prove who they are without certificates. This RFC explains what that secret can and cannot protect, shows how sharing a key or making it too short breaks the protection, and gives applications four concrete rules to follow.

subtitle: When a secret agreed in advance can safely secure TLS 1.3, and the rules that keep it safe.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 can authenticate with keys that were provisioned out of band, but nothing told applications how to choose and manage those keys without weakening the protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9257 explains that PSK security assumes each key is known to exactly one client and one server, shows the attacks that follow when a key is shared or has low entropy, and gives four recommendations for applications.
tldr.outcome: Use keys of at least 128 bits with at least 128 bits of entropy, combine them with an ephemeral key exchange, restrict each key to two logical nodes, and use external PSK importers so the main key can be deleted afterwards.

facts.label: Nodes per PSK
facts.value: At most two logical nodes, one client and one server

facts.label: Pairwise keys for n IoT devices

today: RFC 9257 is an Informational RFC published in July 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is written to be used with RFC 9258, which defines the external PSK importers the recommendations rely on, and it notes that recommended PAKEs for low-entropy keys were still being worked on at the time of writing.

sections.title: What an External PSK Is
sections.content:
This document gives guidance on the use of external Pre-Shared Keys in Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3. The guidance also applies to Datagram TLS (DTLS) 1.3 and Compact TLS 1.3; for readability the document uses the term TLS for all of them.

External PSKs are symmetric secret keys provided to the TLS implementation as external inputs. They are provisioned out of band, which means they are put in place by some other means than the TLS handshake itself, for example typed into two devices or copied onto them from another system.

The document lists the TLS security properties provided by PSKs under certain assumptions, and demonstrates how violating those assumptions leads to attacks. It also discusses PSK use cases, provisioning processes and the support needed in the TLS stack, and it gives advice for applications in various use cases so they can meet the assumptions. The gap it sets out to close is that there is plenty of guidance on generating and verifying passwords, but no equivalent for external PSKs in TLS.

Two definitions matter for the rest of the document. A logical node is a computing presence that other parties can interact with via TLS; one logical node can be realized as several physical instances under common administrative control, such as a server farm. An endpoint is a client or server participating in a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A pre-shared key is a secret both sides already know. In TLS 1.3 it can replace certificates as a way of proving identity. The catch is that a secret is only as safe as the assumptions about who holds it, and this RFC spells those assumptions out.

sections.title: What Happens When a Key Is Shared
sections.content:
Using an established PSK lets TLS nodes authenticate each other's identities. It also brings other benefits, including resistance to attacks in the presence of quantum computers. It does not provide privacy of the endpoint identities, and it does not provide non-repudiation, since one endpoint in a connection can deny the conversation.

PSK authentication implicitly assumes one fundamental property: each PSK is known to exactly one client and one server, and they never swap roles. When several clients or several servers share a PSK naively, with all members holding a common key, TLS authenticates only group membership and the security of the system is brittle in several ways. Any group member can impersonate any other group member. If the PSK is combined with the result of a fresh ephemeral key exchange, then compromising one group member lets the attacker passively read traffic and actively modify it. If the PSK is not combined with a fresh ephemeral key exchange, compromising any group member lets the attacker passively read all traffic, including past traffic, and modify it.

A malicious non-member can also reroute handshakes between honest group members. With three peers A, B and C that all know the PSK, the attack runs as follows: A sends a ClientHello to B; the attacker intercepts it and redirects it to C; C responds with its second flight to A; A sends a Finished message to B, having completed the handshake, ostensibly with B; the attacker redirects that Finished message to C, and C has completed the handshake with A. Peer authentication is not provided. If C supports a weaker set of cipher suites than B, cryptographic algorithm downgrade attacks might also be possible.

This rerouting is a type of identity misbinding attack. The Selfie attack is a special case of it against a group member that can act as both a TLS server and a client: a malicious non-member reroutes a connection from the client to the server on the same endpoint. A partial mitigation for this class of attack is that each group member includes the Server Name Indication extension and terminates the connection when the presented name does not match its own identity.

Sharing also has operational costs. Revoking one group member is not possible without establishing a new PSK for every member that has not been revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: If three machines share one key, TLS can no longer tell them apart, so any one of them can pretend to be another. An attacker who can move messages around can also make two honest machines talk to each other by mistake, and the machines will believe they are talking to the person they intended. Sharing also means you cannot revoke one machine's access without replacing the key everywhere.

sections.title: How Much Randomness the Key Needs
sections.content:
The entropy properties of an external PSK affect the security properties TLS can provide. With a high-entropy PSK, PSK-only key establishment modes give the expected security properties for TLS: the same session keys at both peers, secrecy of the session keys, peer authentication and downgrade protection. Those modes lack forward security, which can be achieved by using a PSK-DH mode or by using PSKs with short lifetimes.

With a low-entropy PSK the picture is worse. PSK-only key establishment modes are subject to passive exhaustive search attacks, which reveal the traffic keys. PSK-DH modes are subject to active attacks in which the attacker impersonates one side. The exhaustive search phase of those attacks can be mounted offline if the attacker captures a single handshake using the PSK, but they will not compromise the traffic keys for that connection, because those keys also depend on the Diffie-Hellman exchange. Low-entropy keys are only secure against active attack if a Password-Authenticated Key Exchange is used with TLS. At the time of writing the Crypto Forum Research Group was working on specifying recommended PAKEs for the symmetric and asymmetric cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A key made of random bits behaves differently from a short guessable one. With a random key, TLS can establish a session on its own, though it cannot protect old traffic if the key later leaks. With a guessable key, an attacker can try every possibility offline and read the session, unless the session also depends on a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange.

sections.title: How External PSKs Are Used and Provisioned
sections.content:
PSK cipher suites were first specified for TLS in 2005, and PSKs are now an integral part of the TLS 1.3 specification, which also uses them for session resumption and distinguishes those resumption PSKs from external PSKs provisioned out of band.

The use cases listed for pairwise external PSKs, shared between one server and one client, include device-to-device communication with out-of-band synchronized keys, where the identity to use is discovered through a different online protocol; intra-data-center communication within a single data center or Point of Presence, mainly to support TLS connections with early data; certificateless server-to-server communication, mainly to avoid the overhead of provisioning and managing PKI certificates; Internet of Things devices with limited computational capability, where the TLS and DTLS profiles for resource-constrained devices suggest PSK cipher suites and the LwM2M specification says servers must support the PSK mode of DTLS; securing RADIUS with TLS, where PSK cipher suites are optional; 3GPP server-to-user equipment authentication; smart cards, where the German electronic identity card supports card-holder authentication to online services with TLS PSK; and quantum resistance, where some deployments use PSKs, or combine them with certificate-based authentication, for the protection they give against quantum computers.

Some use cases do share a PSK between more than two entities. Group chats are one example, where participants may be provisioned a PSK out of band for establishing authenticated connections with other members. IoT devices are another, where the same setting can use one key for n devices, n keys for n devices, or pairwise keys for n^2 combinations.

Provisioning depends on the system and its threat model. Whenever possible, sharing a PSK between nodes should be avoided, though it is sometimes unavoidable, and when it happens the accommodations of Section 6 should be used. Many industrial protocols distribute PSKs by hand, either by typing the key into the devices or by a trust-on-first-use approach in which a device is unprotected until the first login, which matters because many devices have a very limited interface, sometimes only a numeric keypad. Some devices provision PSKs through an out-of-band cloud-based syncing protocol, and some secrets are baked into hardware or software at manufacturing time, printed on labels or included in a Bill of Materials for easy scanning or import.

Provisioning systems are often constrained in application-specific ways. Although one goal is to ensure that each pair of nodes has a unique key, some systems do not want to distribute pairwise shared keys, and some require the provisioning process to embed application-specific information in the PSKs or their identities. Identities may sometimes need to be routable.
sections.plainLanguage: External keys are used wherever running a certificate system is too heavy: small devices, machines talking inside one data center, card readers and mobile networks. How the key gets onto the devices varies, from typing it in to a keypad to syncing it through a cloud service or printing it on a label at the factory. The document's advice is to give each pair of devices its own key whenever the system allows it.

sections.title: Four Recommendations for Applications
sections.content:
The recommended requirements for applications using external PSKs are stated as four numbered rules.

  1. Each PSK SHOULD be derived from at least 128 bits of entropy, MUST be at least 128 bits long, and SHOULD be combined with an ephemeral key exchange, for example by using the psk_dhe_ke Pre-Shared Key Exchange Mode in TLS 1.3 for forward secrecy. Low-entropy PSKs, those derived from less than 128 bits of entropy, are subject to attack and SHOULD be avoided. If only low-entropy keys are available, key establishment mechanisms such as PAKE that mitigate the risk of offline dictionary attacks SHOULD be employed; no such mechanism has yet been standardized, and they will not necessarily follow the same architecture as the external PSK import process.
  2. Unless other accommodations are made to mitigate the risks of PSKs known to a group, each PSK MUST be restricted in its use to at most two logical nodes: one in a TLS client role and one in a TLS server role. The two logical nodes MAY be the same, in different roles. Two acceptable accommodations are described in RFC 9258: exchanging client and server identifiers over the TLS connection after the handshake, and incorporating identifiers for both the client and the server into the context string for an external PSK importer.
  3. Nodes SHOULD use external PSK importers when configuring PSKs for a client-server pair, where applicable. Importers make provisioning easier and less error-prone by deriving a unique imported PSK from the external PSK for each key derivation function a node supports.
  4. Where possible, the main PSK, the one fed into the importer, SHOULD be deleted after the imported keys have been generated. This prevents an attacker from bootstrapping a compromise of one node into the ability to attack connections between any node, since otherwise the attacker can recover the main key and re-run the importer.

The document then describes the stack interfaces that applications use to configure external PSKs, and the details differ between implementations. OpenSSL and BoringSSL let applications specify support for external PSKs through distinct cipher suites in TLS 1.2 and below and configure callbacks invoked for PSK selection during the handshake, which must provide a PSK identity and key; the PSK length is validated to be between 1 and 256 bytes and the identity may be up to 128 bytes long. mbedTLS client applications configure PSKs before creating a connection by giving the identity and value inline, servers implement callbacks like OpenSSL's, and both the identity and the key may be between 1 and 16 bytes long. gnuTLS takes raw byte strings or hexadecimal strings and does not validate the identity or key size, and wolfSSL uses callbacks similar to OpenSSL's.

PSK identities have their own rules. RFC 4279 requires the identity to be converted to a character string and then encoded to octets with UTF-8, to avoid interoperability problems when a human typed it in, while the profile for constrained devices advises against assuming any structured format and recommends byte-by-byte comparison. TLS 1.3 treats the identity as a sequence of opaque bytes, shown in its specification as opaque identity<1..2^16-1>, compared byte by byte and required to be at least 1 byte and at most 65535 bytes long. An identity MAY be a user-configured string, as in Extensible Authentication Protocol deployments where gnuTLS treats identities as usernames, and MAY have a domain name suffix for roaming and federation, which is NOT RECOMMENDED where that suffix is privacy sensitive. Deployments should take care that the identity is long enough to avoid collisions.

Collisions with resumption PSK identities are possible, though unlikely. When a server receives a PSK identity in a TLS 1.3 ClientHello, some stacks run the application's callback before checking the internal session resumption cache, so an external PSK usually takes precedence. Because resumption PSK identities are assigned by the stack, it is RECOMMENDED that they be assigned in a way that lets them be distinguished from external PSKs.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are short: a long random key, combined with a fresh key exchange, used by only two machines, imported through the standard mechanism and then thrown away. The rest of the section is about the practical detail of how each TLS library takes the key, and about the name attached to it, which travels in the clear and must therefore not be something secret.

sections.title: Privacy, Identities and Early Data
sections.content:
PSK privacy properties are orthogonal to the security properties described earlier. TLS does little to keep PSK identity information private: the identifier appears in cleartext in a ClientHello, so an adversary learns information about the external PSK or its identifier, and a passive adversary can link two or more connections that use the same external PSK on the wire. Depending on the identity, a passive attacker may also be able to identify the device, person or enterprise running the client or the server. An active attacker can use the PSK identity to suppress handshakes or application data from a specific device by blocking, delaying or rate-limiting its traffic. Techniques for mitigating these risks need further analysis and are out of scope. External PSKs are also intrinsically linkable by PSK receivers, since servers can link successive connections that use the same external PSK.

The security considerations repeat the concerns about proper identification of TLS 1.3 endpoints and the extra risks when external PSKs are known to a group. It is NOT RECOMMENDED to share the same PSK between more than one client and server, although application scenarios may rely on doing so. RFC 9258 helps mitigate rerouting and Selfie-style reflection attacks when a PSK is shared among multiple nodes, by using node identifiers correctly in the ImportedIdentity.context construct. One solution would be for each endpoint to select one globally unique identifier for use in all its PSK handshakes, for example one of its MAC addresses, a 32-byte random number or its UUID; such persistent global identifiers carry privacy implications.

Each endpoint SHOULD know the identifier of the other endpoint it wants to connect to and SHOULD compare it with the identifier that endpoint used. Endpoints sharing the same group PSK can, however, always impersonate each other.

One last point concerns early data. When early data is used with an external PSK, the random value in the ClientHello is the only source of entropy contributing to key diversity between sessions, so when an external PSK is used more than once the client's random number source has a significant role in the protection of the early data.
sections.plainLanguage: The name attached to the key is sent in the open, so it identifies the device and lets an observer tell that two connections used the same key. That is why the document warns against putting anything sensitive in the identity, and why a shared key is only safe if each side also checks the other's name, and even then any member of the group can still impersonate any other.

viz.caption: THE FOUR RECOMMENDATIONS FOR EXTERNAL PSK USE

items.label: Length and entropy
items.desc: At least 128 bits long, derived from at least 128 bits of entropy, and combined with an ephemeral key exchange for forward secrecy.

items.label: One client and one server
items.desc: Each PSK restricted to at most two logical nodes, unless other accommodations are made for a group of PSK holders.

items.label: Use an importer
items.desc: Nodes should use external PSK importers, which derive a unique imported PSK for each key derivation function the node supports.

items.label: Delete the main PSK
items.desc: Where possible, delete the main PSK once the imported keys have been generated.
